opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when we started, most of the team had never trained a large model end to end. Many were very young, some were fresh graduates or interns, and their experience was mostly in research papers or smaller-scale work. So I didn't treat Flash only as a product goal. I treated it as a training ground, a way for the team to grow by actually doing the whole thing.

My basic belief is that you can't learn large models by watching. You have to touch every part: data, pretraining, infrastructure, post-training, evaluation. So with Flash, we deliberately kept the scope manageable. A smaller, faster model meant shorter iteration cycles. If an experiment failed, we'd know within days, not months, and people could form intuition quickly. That feedback loop matters a lot for an inexperienced team.

The second thing was giving people real ownership. I didn't want a structure where a few senior people make all the decisions and everyone else just runs scripts. Young people often have very good taste and a lot of courage, they just haven't been given the chance. So I let them own important pieces, even if they made mistakes. Mistakes were expected. What I cared about was whether they understood *why* something went wrong and could explain it clearly.

Third, I tried to build a culture of being very honest with results. In large models it's easy to fool yourself: you look at a benchmark, it goes up, you feel happy. But I kept pushing everyone to ask whether an improvement was real, whether it generalized, whether we really understood the cause. That kind of rigor is something you only build by practicing it together, project after project.

And finally, I think the team needed to believe they could do it. At the beginning there was a lot of self-doubt, like, "Can we really compete with teams that have done this for years?" Shipping Flash gave them that confidence. Once people see that something they built actually works and is used, their mindset changes completely. For me, that change in the team was maybe more important than the model itself.

fable-5.1.text:
When I first took over the team, honestly, most of the people hadn't trained a large model end to end before. A lot of them came from very strong academic backgrounds, or from smaller-scale work, but they'd never been through the full cycle of a serious pretraining run — the data pipeline, the infra fights, the sleepless nights watching a loss curve that looks slightly wrong. And you can't teach that in a reading group. You can only learn it by doing it, and by doing it on something that actually matters.

So that was really the thinking behind Flash. I didn't want our first project to be a toy. I also didn't want it to be so enormous that one mistake would burn months of compute and destroy everyone's confidence. Flash sat in the middle: a model that was small enough that we could iterate fast and make mistakes cheaply, but real enough that it had to ship, had to be benchmarked publicly, and had to be something we were willing to put our names on.

A few things I was very deliberate about.

The first was ownership. I split the work into vertical pieces — data, pretraining, post-training, infra, evaluation — and for each piece there was one person whose name was on it. Not a committee. If something broke in data, everyone knew who to go to, and that person knew they couldn't hide behind the team. That sounds harsh, but it's actually the fastest way for people to grow. When you own something, you start thinking about it in the shower.

The second was that I insisted everyone touch the full pipeline at least once, even if their main job was a narrow slice. The evaluation person had to run a small pretraining job. The infra person had to go through an SFT round. Because in this field, the biggest mistakes happen at the seams between stages. If you don't understand what the next person downstream needs from you, you'll optimize your own corner and hurt the whole model.

The third thing — and this is maybe the most important — I tried very hard to make failure cheap and visible. We had a lot of runs that didn't work. We'd kill them, write a short postmortem, and share it with the whole team the same day. No blame, just: here's what we tried, here's what the curve looked like, here's what we think happened. After a couple months, people stopped being afraid of a bad run. They started treating it as data. That shift, from "I don't want to be the one who broke it" to "let's find out why it broke," is really the moment a team becomes a real large-model team.

And I'll be honest, I was also learning. My experience before this had been in a very different environment, with a lot of existing infrastructure and very senior people around me. Here I had to make calls about compute allocation, about when to stop a run, about what to cut from the roadmap, with much less margin for error. So in a way Flash was training me too.

By the time we finished, the model itself was fine — it did what we needed it to do. But the real output of Flash wasn't the checkpoint. It was that I now had a team where every person had been through one full cycle, had owned something, had broken something and fixed it. The second project went maybe three times faster, not because anyone got smarter, but because we'd already paid the tuition.

astra-6.text:
I approached Flash as both a project we needed to deliver and an opportunity for the team to learn. With an inexperienced team, you can’t expect everyone to understand the whole system immediately. You need to break the work into concrete problems, give people ownership, and help them develop judgment through experiments.

The important thing was to go beyond asking whether an experiment worked. Why did it work? If it failed, what did that tell us? What should we test next? That process helps people move from following instructions to making independent decisions.

I also think you have to balance support with room to explore. If you prescribe every step, people may complete the task without learning how to approach the next one. For me, developing the team meant gradually giving them more responsibility as their understanding grew.

sol-6.1.text:
I approached Flash as both a research project and a way for the team to learn through practice. With an inexperienced team, you can’t expect everyone to know how to tackle an open-ended problem immediately. You need to make the goal clear, break it into concrete questions, and give people ownership of those questions.

I tried to provide enough guidance to help them get started without making every decision for them. We would discuss why an experiment was worth doing, what we could learn from the result, and what to try next. The important thing was to develop their judgment, rather than simply have them execute a list of tasks.

As people gained experience, they could take responsibility for larger problems. For me, that was a central part of developing the team: doing the project together while gradually enabling people to work independently.
